purpose: What changes when a light-source photon has a shorter wavelength?
meaning: For an ideal monochromatic photon in vacuum, frequency f and wavelength λ satisfy fλ=c, and photon energy in joules is E_J=hf. The speed of light c and Planck constant h have exact SI defining values. Divide the joule reading by the exact conversion u=1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ joules per electronvolt to obtain its electronvolt reading E. Shorter wavelength gives higher frequency and higher energy per photon; it does not by itself specify beam brightness or power. The unit of h is the joule second.

definition.setting: A light-source designer compares photons from ideal monochromatic emitters. Change the vacuum wavelength λ in nanometres. The wave spacing marks that physical length on a fixed ruler; the energy bar independently measures the energy carried by one photon.

conditions: Vacuum wavelength is 400–800 nanometres. Substitute that same wavelength in metres in f=c/λ. The physical model is one ideal monochromatic photon obeying E_J=hf, with exact SI c=299792458 m/s and h=6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J·s, and exact u=1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ J/eV.
definition.domain_notes: The oscillation indicates wavelength only: its height is arbitrary and represents neither photon trajectory, probability amplitude nor brightness. Energy per photon differs from beam power and photon arrival rate. Dispersion in materials, emission bandwidth and interactions with matter are outside this model. Numerical readings approximate the analytic expressions.
